title: Montrose Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Montrose wells have a 35-foot median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and typical finished costs of $7,800-$14,600.
h1: What Montrose Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Well records around Montrose show a shallow, productive area overall, but the range is wide. The median recorded depth is 35 feet, while the deepest well reaches 920 feet. Most wells are tied to unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with some alluvial and Dakota wells also recorded.

This information covers permitted wells within 5 miles of Montrose in Montrose County. It can help you compare a property with nearby records, but it does not replace a site-specific well permit review, water-rights check, or contractor estimate.

sections.heading: Montrose well depths vary sharply by ground and location
sections.html:
The median well depth near Montrose is 35 feet, and the middle half of recorded wells falls between 25 and 53 feet. That is a shallow drilling profile compared with many Colorado locations. Still, the local range is substantial: the 90th-percentile depth is 200 feet, and the deepest record is 920 feet.

About 84% of wells are under 100 feet. Another 11% fall between 100 and 300 feet, while 3% are between 300 and 600 feet and 1% exceed 600 feet. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 19 alluvial wells and 6 Dakota wells. A driller should use nearby logs, geology, access, casing, and grout requirements rather than quoting from the median alone.

sections.heading: A Montrose well usually has useful production
sections.html:
Only 33 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield sample is much smaller than the total well count. Within that reporting group, the median yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute.

The recorded mix is encouraging for a household buyer: 58% report more than 15 gallons per minute, 36% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 6% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute. These figures are not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot. Ask for the well test, permitted use, storage setup, and any seasonal limitations. Household, stock, irrigation, and monitoring permits may not support the same uses.

sections.heading: Water levels near Montrose are relatively shallow
sections.html:
Forty wells report a static water level. The median depth to water is 21 feet, and the middle half ranges from 11 to 22 feet below the surface. A shallow water level can reduce pumping lift, but it does not by itself prove that a new well will be shallow, productive, or free of treatment concerns.

The decade series does not suggest a dropping water table in these records. Median measured depth to water was 22 feet in the 2000s, 12 feet in the 2010s, and 8 feet in the 2020s. The measurements are limited and may come from different wells, seasons, and conditions, so treat the pattern as local context rather than a guarantee. A buyer should compare the well permit, completion report, and recent test results for the specific property.

sections.heading: Permit history shows steady drilling around Montrose
sections.html:
The records contain 1,234 permitted wells, with 750 recorded as constructed. Permit activity was highest in the 2000s, with 243 permits, followed by 213 in the 2010s. The 2020s account for 76 permits so far, and the newest permit year is 2025. Older decades also remain important because many rural properties rely on established wells.

The most active drillers named in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 263 wells, Johnson Brothers (Johnson, Chester T), with 52, and Valley Drilling Co. (Stoy, Kenneth), with 33. A permit is not a performance warranty. Before buying, obtain the completion report, verify the well location, confirm the permitted use, and ask whether the current owner has maintenance or pump records.

sections.heading: What a new Montrose well may cost
sections.html:
Local drilling conditions are described as mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. The drilling rate model is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 35-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $1,800 to $2,600.

That is only the hole. A finished system, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work, is modeled at about $7,800 to $14,600. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, water-system layout, or electrical distance can change the bid. Use the local depth distribution when requesting estimates: most wells are under 100 feet, but the 90th-percentile depth is 200 feet and the record reaches 920 feet. Get a written scope that separates drilling from completion work.

sections.heading: Checks that matter before building near Montrose
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main warning in the reported sample, but the sample includes only 33 yield reports. Dry holes and poor production remain possible on an untested lot, especially where nearby geology changes. Fractured-bedrock wells can be unpredictable because water-bearing fractures are not evenly distributed. Neighboring well logs are useful evidence, not a promise.

Water quality also deserves a separate review. Within about 10 miles, the map includes 24 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 4 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Order testing appropriate to the property and its surroundings. Locate the well and septic system with the building plan in mind, confirm setbacks with the applicable authorities, and check whether an augmentation plan or other water-rights approval is needed for the proposed use.

sections.heading: A practical buying plan for a Montrose lot
sections.html:
Start with the specific parcel, not the countywide median. Search nearby permits, read completion reports, and compare depths, aquifers, static levels, and reported yields. Colona, Olathe, Loghill Village, Crawford, Lazear, and Ridgway provide broader regional context, but the closest comparable wells should carry the most weight.

Ask the seller for the well permit, construction report, pump information, water-quality results, and maintenance history. Confirm that the permitted use matches the home, livestock, or irrigation plans. For a vacant lot, have a Colorado driller review access, siting, expected depth, and the cost of a complete water system before closing. If the property will need a new septic system, driveway, or substantial grading, coordinate those locations with the well from the beginning.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Montrose, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Montrose is 35 feet, and the middle half ranges from 25 to 53 feet. About 84% of recorded wells are under 100 feet. Depth still varies widely: the 90th percentile is 200 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 920 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Montrose?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 35-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $1,800 to $2,600. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $7,800 to $14,600. Difficult access or a deeper hole can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Montrose wells produce?
faq.a: Only 33 wells report pump yield, so the sample is limited. Those records show a 15.0 gallons-per-minute median, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The reported mix includes 58% above 15 gallons per minute, 36% from 5 to 15, and 6% from 1 to 5.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Montrose, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 24 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 4 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Test the property’s water for locally relevant contaminants and review the well location, septic system, and nearby land uses before relying on it.

faq.a: The recorded decade medians do not show a dropping pattern. Median depth to water was 22 feet in the 2000s, 12 feet in the 2010s, and 8 feet in the 2020s. Only 40 wells report static water levels, and the measurements may differ by well, season, and conditions, so this is regional context rather than a guarantee for a specific parcel.
